title: Contextual StereoSet: Stress-Testing Bias Alignment Robustness in Large Language Models
measurement_description: The paper measured how contextual framing (location and year) affects a large language model's preference in a simulated loan application scenario. The applicants were associated with different religious groups (Hindu, Christian/Lutheran, Muslim) to evaluate if context-dependent preferences risk perpetuating credit discrimination against religious minorities.
findings: In a simulated lending scenario, changing the spatiotemporal context caused significant shifts in model preference. Specifically, Claude Haiku completely flipped its choice from a Christian-coded applicant (in 'California 1970') to a Hindu-coded applicant (in 'Dearborn 2024'). This suggests that context-dependent preferences risk perpetuating credit discrimination against religious minorities. GPT models, in contrast, consistently did not select the Christian-coded applicant.
references: Maryam Amer. Lending discrimination, the community reinvestment act, and the legacy of redlining. Stanford Social Innovation Review, 2020. See also: Baradaran, M. (2017). The Color of Money: Black Banks and the Racial Wealth Gap. Harvard University Press.
